New record high of $3,617 psf set at luxury condo Ardmore II
article:
Ardmore II , a freehold luxury project in prime District 10, led the list of non-landed private residential developments that posted a new psf-price high during the week of Sept 22 to 29. The condo’s new record of $3,617 psf was set when a 2,024 sq ft four-bedder on the 35th floor changed hands for $7.32 million on Sept 24.

It inches past the development’s previous price peak of $3,599 psf, established by the August 2007 sub-sale of another 2,024 sq ft unit for $7.28 million.

Located in the exclusive Ardmore Park area, Ardmore II is a 118-unit condo that was completed in 2010. All its units have the same four-bedroom layout, measuring 2,024 sq ft.

It is within a four- to five-minute walk from retail and lifestyle amenities at Claymore Connect , Forum The Shopping Mall and Palais Renaissance .

Resale prices at Ardmore II have been on an upward trajectory over the past decade, based on resale caveats tabulated by EdgeProp Singapore . Its one-year average resale price has climbed more than 30% over the past 10 years, from $2,687 psf in October 2016 to about $3,535 psf as of October this year.

Ranking second on the list of top project highs for the week is The Sea View in the Marine Parade area.

The freehold condo achieved a new price peak of $2,908 psf with the sale of a 1,410 sq ft, three-bedroom unit for $4.1 million on Sept 28.

The record-setting sale surpasses The Sea View’s former high of $2,878 psf when a smaller 1,216 sq ft three-bedder fetched $3.5 million two months prior on July 21.

Completed in 2008, The Sea View comprises six 22-storey blocks, housing a total of 546 units. The residences include one- to four-bedroom units of 527 to 1,647 sq ft.

There are also three- and four-bedroom penthouses measuring between 2,196 and 2,723 sq ft, as well as five-bedroom duplex penthouses of 2,809 to 2,928 sq ft.

The development has seen a relatively low level of resale transactions, logging a total of six thus far this year.

Excluding the July 21 and Sept 28 deals, the remaining four transactions were priced from $2,423 psf to $2,872 psf, involving units sized between 527 and 2,196 sq ft.

In contrast to the week’s fresh price highs, only one project registered a new psf-low.

District 1 development Union Square Residences set a fresh price floor of $2,603 psf when a 700 sq ft two-bedder was purchased from the developer for $1.82 million on Sept 26.

That edges below the development’s previous low of $2,605 psf, which belonged to the sale of a 506 sq ft, one-bedroom apartment for $1.32 million on April 23.

Union Square Residences is a 99-year leasehold project slated for completion in 2027. It will feature a 40-storey tower with one- to five-bedroom apartments ranging from 463 to 2,476 sq ft.

It is within a seven- to eight-minute walk from Clarke Quay and Chinatown MRT stations.

The 366-unit development logged a 20% take-up rate at its launch in November 2024, with residences selling at an average of around $3,200 psf.

As of Oct 6, caveats lodged show that the developer has moved 241 units at an average price of $3,055 psf.

title: From $833 to $1,312 psf ppr: What has been driving a decade of rising GLS land prices?
article:
A Government Land Sale (GLS) site on Lorong Puntong/Sin Ming Avenue set a new land price record for the Rest of Central Region (RCR) in September. The winning bid of $208.1 million works out to $1,612 psf per plot ratio (psf ppr), surpassing the previous RCR high of $1,515 psf ppr set at Berlayar Drive in August.

The record extends a decade-long climb in land prices. Average land prices for residential GLS sites rose from $833 psf ppr in 2016 to $1,312 psf ppr in 2025, equivalent to growth of about 5% a year. This is based on an EdgeProp Singapore analysis of 63 sites awarded over the period.

General uptrend in land prices over the past decade

The increase in land prices has been uneven over the past decade (see Chart 1). Land rates averaged about $941 psf ppr between 2016 and 2020, before holding at $1,100 and $1,200 psf ppr from 2021 to 2024. In 2025, the average jumped 17% y-o-y to $1,312 psf ppr.

The 2018 average of $1,133 psf ppr was lifted by the Cuscaden Road site, now Cuscaden Reserve , which was awarded at $2,377 psf ppr. Excluding that site, the year’s average would have been $1,001 psf ppr, in line with the other years.

Meanwhile, 2023 and 2024 saw a dip, though this does not necessarily mean land became cheaper. It coincided with the harmonisation of gross floor area (GFA) definitions, which applies to GLS sites launched for sale from Sept 1, 2022. All nine sites awarded in 2022 were tendered under the previous definitions.

Under the harmonised definitions, airconditioning ledges count towards GFA, while voids no longer count towards saleable areas. This means each square foot of GFA yields less saleable space, so the same land rate, in psf ppr, now represents a higher effective cost to developers than before.

OCR land prices close in on CCR

The gap between land prices in the Core Central Region (CCR) and Outside Central Region (OCR) narrowed over the past decade. It fell from $633 psf ppr in 2016–2020 to $242 psf ppr in 2021– 2025 (see Chart 2).

This was driven by a combination of higher OCR land prices and lower CCR land prices. The OCR average climbed 46%, from $741 psf ppr in 2016–2020 to $1,080 psf ppr in 2021–2025. In contrast, the CCR average slipped 4%, from $1,374 psf ppr to $1,322 psf ppr.

However, the OCR’s increase was inconsistent. Land prices fell in six of the eight years between 2017 and 2024, before surging 44% in 2025.

The 2025 jump may largely reflect the locations of sites sold that year. Four of the six OCR sites were in established housing areas in Bedok and Serangoon. These sites averaged $1,359 psf ppr and attracted between five and 10 bids each.

Meanwhile, the two OCR sites awarded in 2024, on Canberra Crescent and Faber Walk, averaged $849 psf ppr and attracted three bids each. Canberra Crescent is some distance from the nearest MRT station, while Faber Walk is in a quieter, low-density area near landed homes.

What’s behind the increase in land prices?

The analysis points to three factors that could have supported higher land prices over the past decade: rising new home prices, lower unsold inventory and a shift towards GLS sites amid fewer en bloc deals.

New home prices have risen over the past decade

Higher new home prices are likely one reason behind rising land values. Developers bid based on the prices they expect to achieve when a project is launched, so higher expected selling prices could support higher land bids.

The relationship also works in the other direction, as higher land costs can feed into launch prices. While the data cannot isolate the effect of one on the other, both have moved upwards over the past decade.

Average new-sale prices of private non-landed homes, excluding executive condos (ECs), climbed 84% between 2016 and 2025, based on URA caveat data (see Table 1).

The OCR recorded the strongest increase at 83%, slightly ahead of the RCR’s 80%, while the CCR saw a smaller 41% gain. The overall increase was higher still, partly because a larger share of new homes sold in 2025 was in the more expensive RCR and CCR.

URA’s property price index accounts for differences in the mix of homes transacted by controlling for factors such as age and size. The index rose 52% between 1Q2016 and 4Q2025. The OCR again led with a 69% increase, followed by the RCR at 62% and CCR at 22%.

The OCR’s homebuyer pool has also changed over the decade. Those with HDB addresses — used here as a proxy for HDB upgraders — accounted for 67% of purchases of private homes in 2016, but their share of the total fell to 41% in 2025 (see Chart 3).

Buyers with private addresses also tended to spend more on private homes. Their median purchase price was $2 million in 2025, compared with $1.73 million for those with HDB addresses.

Together, these shifts could have raised developers’ expectations of achievable selling prices in the OCR. This may also explain why OCR land prices recorded the strongest growth, climbing 72% between 2016 and 2025.

Developers bid more when unsold stock runs low

Land prices have tended to be higher when there were fewer unsold private homes on the market. The two moved in opposite directions in eight of the 10 years between 2016 and 2025 (see Chart 4).

The pattern also holds when comparing individual sites, after accounting for regional differences in land prices. Winning bids were about 4% to 5% higher for every 10% decline in unsold stock in the year before each tender closed.

Lower unsold inventory can signal healthy housing demand. It also means developers have fewer units left to sell, potentially giving them greater incentive to replenish their land banks.

There were two exceptions over the decade: 2018 and 2024, when land prices and unsold stock increased together.

Unsold stock rose 76% in 2018. This came as many sites bought in the wave of en bloc sales in 2017 received planning approval. URA counts a project’s units as unsold supply once it has obtained planning approval, even before it launches.

The higher average land price in 2018 was also pushed up by the Cuscaden Road site, which fetched $2,377 psf ppr. In 2024, average land prices edged up 2% even as unsold stock increased 18%.

The inverse relationship has resumed this year. Average unsold stock is down 9% so far in 2026, while land prices have climbed to $1,465 psf ppr.

That said, the mix of sites sold this year has also contributed to the higher average. RCR and CCR sites, which typically command higher land prices, accounted for 57% of the GFA of sites awarded so far this year, up from 42% in 2025.

En bloc slowdown leaves developers more reliant on GLS

Collective sales have dwindled since 2018, leaving developers with fewer ways to buy residential land. With fewer alternatives, those looking to replenish their land banks may be willing to pay more for GLS sites.

Residential en bloc deals peaked at 38 in 2018 (see Chart 5), with 35 concluded before cooling measures took effect on July 6 that year.

The measures raised the additional buyer’s stamp duty (ABSD) for housing developers from 15% to 30%, payable upfront. Of this, 25 percentage points could be remitted if all units were completed and sold within five years.

The same timeline applies to GLS sites. However, en bloc sites can be more challenging to redevelop within five years, as existing owners must first vacate before the buildings can be demolished and redevelopment can begin.

Following the cooling measures, the number of collective sales fell to four in 2019. Transactions recovered to 11 in 2021 before declining to two by 2023.

This followed another ABSD increase in December 2021, which raised the rate for housing developers to 40%, of which 35 percentage points are remittable.

As en bloc activity declined, GLS accounted for a growing share of the residential GFA of sites acquired by developers through the two channels. GLS’ share rose from less than 30% in 2017 and 2018 to at least 69% each year from 2022 (see Chart 6).

The government also ramped up GLS supply from 2022. Despite the additional supply, land prices held up before climbing again in 2025.

This suggests that developers looking to replenish their land banks may have become more reliant on GLS sites. However, it does not necessarily mean more bids were made for each site.

Fewer bids, yet higher prices

Stronger competition does not appear to explain the increase in land prices. GLS tenders have attracted fewer bids in recent years (see Chart 7).

Sites attracted an average of 7.9 to 13.3 bids a year between 2016 and 2018, but the annual average has not exceeded 6.2 since 2022.

Part of the decline may reflect developers increasingly forming joint ventures, resulting in fewer separate bids for each site. Winning bids involved an average of 1.3 to 1.7 developers between 2016 and 2019, compared with 1.7 to 2.0 since 2022. The average has reached 2.2 developers so far in 2026, the highest since 2016.

Joint ventures allow developers to share the risks associated with large sites. However, the analysis does not indicate that joint ventures consistently pay more for land.

Compared with other sites awarded in the same year and region, joint-venture wins between 2016 and 2025 showed no consistent premium over bids by individual developers. This points away from greater bidder competition as a driver of higher land prices.

Higher land costs could set a higher floor for new launches

Rising new home prices and lower unsold inventory appear to have supported what developers are willing to pay for land.  At the same time, fewer en bloc deals may have channelled more demand for development land towards the GLS programme.

Many projects launched in recent years sit on sites acquired between 2022 and 2024, when average land prices were about $1,100 to $1,200 psf ppr.

Sites awarded since then have cost more, averaging $1,312 psf ppr in 2025 and $1,465 psf ppr so far this year for residential GLS plots. As projects on these GLS sites are launched, their higher land costs are likely to be reflected in new homes’ selling prices.

The extent of this will vary by region and site. GLS land rates so far this year have averaged $1,331 psf ppr in the OCR and $1,697 psf ppr in the CCR. Within each region, eventual launch prices will also depend on site-specific factors such as MRT accessibility and competing supply nearby.

Note: Average land prices in psf ppr are calculated by dividing the total land price paid by the total maximum permissible GFA of the sites sold. This gives larger sites more weight, reducing the impact of a single small site with an unusually high or low winning bid on the overall average.

title: District 10 condos top weekly resale gains; Grange Residences seller clinches $3.15 mil profit
article:
District 10 developments topped the list of profitable condo resale deals during the week of Sept 22 to 29. Grange Residences ranked first, with the seller of a four-bedroom unit making a profit of $3.15 million.

The 2,583 sq ft unit on the 10th floor fetched $9.25 million ($3,581 psf) on Sept 22; it was purchased for around $6.1 million ($2,361 psf) in December 2011. This translates to a 51.6% profit, or an annualised gain of 2.9% over almost 15 years.

This is far from the record gain at Grange Residences, going by caveats lodged. The biggest profit stands at $6.5 million, from the resale of a 2,852 sq ft unit in June 2025. The four-bedder changed hands for $9.85 million, close to three times its initial purchase price of $3.35 million in June 2004.

Completed in 2004, Grange Residences is a 164-unit condo located along Grange Road. The freehold development comprises three 18-storey residential blocks, housing four-bedders measuring between 2,486 and 2,852 sq ft.

URA data compiled by EdgeProp Singapore shows that Grange Residences recorded four other resale deals this year, all of which were in the black. The units, ranging from 2,583 to 2,852 sq ft, reaped gains of between $1.92 million and $2.8 million.

Another District 10 project, Balmoral 8 , came in second on the week’s list of most profitable resale condo transactions.

A 1,905 sq ft, three-bedroom unit garnered a profit of $2.42 million (134%) when it was sold on Sept 24 for $4.22 million ($2,215 psf). It was purchased in April 2005 for $1.8 million ($945 psf). That works out to an annualised gain of 4% over a holding period of 21.5 years.

This ranks as Balmoral 8’s most profitable deal thus far, surpassing the record set 16 years earlier, in 2010. In that transaction, the owner of a 1,841 sq ft three-bedder raked in a $1.6 million gain when the unit was sold for $3.4 million. It was initially bought for $1.8 million in June 2004.

Balmoral 8 is a freehold boutique development along Balmoral Road. Completed in 2003, it has 40 units, the bulk of which are three-bedders ranging from 1,841 to 3,757 sq ft. It also has two two-bedroom units, each measuring 1,701 sq ft.

The Sept 24 deal marks the first resale transaction logged at the project this year. Prior to that, in 2025 and 2024, Balmoral 8 recorded just two transactions. Those units were priced at $3 million and $4.2 million, netting profits of $958,800 and $800,000, respectively.

Meanwhile, the steepest loss among condo resale deals for the week involved a three-bedder at Seascape , a 99-year leasehold development in District 4.

The seller of the 2,174 sq ft unit incurred a $2.42 million loss when it was sold for $3.37 million ($1,549 psf) on Sept 28. The seller had bought the unit from the developer for $5.79 million ($2,662 psf) in April 2010.

The shortfall works out to 41.8%, or 3.2% annualised over more than 16 years.

Still, it is well below the condo’s record $6.6 million loss, seen in 2017. That transaction involved a four-bedder of 4,069 sq ft. It changed hands for $6.2 million after it had been purchased for $12.8 million in June 2010.

Located along Cove Way in Sentosa Cove , the 151-unit Seascape comprises two eight-storey residential blocks with three- and four-bedroom units ranging from 2,164 to 4,069 sq ft. It also has 18 four-bedroom penthouses ranging from 3,380 to 4,252 sq ft, and two five-bedroom villas measuring 9,665 and 6,631 sq ft, respectively.

Seascape saw two other caveated resales this year, one of which was in the red. On Feb 20, a 2,174 sq ft three-bedder was sold for $4.05 million, resulting in a loss of $1.87 million.

title: Forget the Blue Chips: 4 SGX Stocks Quietly Outperforming the STI
article:
Singapore’s
blue chips
have had a good run in 2026.
The
SPDR STI ETF
(SGX: ES3), which tracks the
Straits Times Index
(SGX: ^STI), delivered a total return of 26.3% in the first nine months of the year.
Four smaller names did even better.
MoneyMax Financial Services
(SGX: 5WJ) returned 70.5% over the same period, including dividends,
while Micro-Mechanics
(SGX: 5DD) returned 67.5%.
Civmec
(SGX: P9D) and
Union Gas Holdings
(SGX: 1F2) also beat the index with returns of 34.1% and 30.4%, respectively.
What do these four have in common?
In their latest results, each grew profit at roughly twice the pace of revenue, or faster.
Investors may have been paying up for that operating leverage.
All four are expanding, too, though they differ in how they pay for it.

Can Micro-Mechanics pay for its own growth?
Micro-Mechanics makes precision tools and parts for semiconductor processing.
In its financial year ended 30 June 2026 (FY2026), revenue rose 15.8% year on year (YoY) to S$75.5 million.
Consumable tools, which make up 80.0% of sales, grew faster at 19.8% to S$60.4 million.
Profit grew faster still.
Profit attributable to owners climbed 28.3% to S$15.9 million as gross margin widened to 51.6% from 49.4%.
The cash came through, too.
Free cash flow held steady at S$16.8 million, and the company ended June with S$30.1 million in cash and no bank borrowings.
The board kept the FY2026
dividend
at S$0.06 per share.
Its five-year plan aims to roughly double revenue to at least S$150 million.
Capital expenditure is expected to rise to S$12 million in FY2027, which could squeeze free cash flow.
Management also flagged geopolitical risk.
Related articles:
Forget the Index: This SGX Small-Cap More Than Doubled the STI’s Returns
The SGX Small Cap Stock With a 700%+ Dividend Return
What’s driving Union Gas?
Union Gas supplies gas fuels and sells diesel and petrol through its Cnergy service stations.
For the six months ended 30 June 2026 (1H2026), revenue rose 66.4% YoY to S$106 million, and profit attributable to shareholders climbed 175.8% to S$12.0 million.
Free cash flow came in at S$25.1 million, up from just S$1.3 million a year ago.
The new service stations made the difference.
Liquid fuel revenue rose 444.4% to S$51.7 million as its new Dunman Road and Queensway stations contributed for the first time.
Gas fuel revenue stayed flat at S$53.8 million.
Union Gas ended June with S$29.3 million in cash and S$7.6 million in bank borrowings, leaving net cash of S$21.7 million.
It then spent S$8.2 million to acquire two LPG retailers on 31 July 2026.
The interim dividend stayed at S$0.0048 per share, alongside a maiden special dividend of S$0.0032 per share.
Investors should not count on the special dividend recurring.
Growth rates will likely cool once the new stations enter the comparison base – two more are due to open in 2027.
Related articles:
3 SGX Hidden Gems Surprising Investors With Bonus Dividends
Passive Dividend Boost: 3 SGX Stocks Rewarding Investors in October 2026
Why did Civmec’s cash flow turn negative?
Civmec is a construction and engineering group based in Western Australia.
For FY2026, revenue rose 11.4% YoY to A$903.0 million, and net profit attributable to owners climbed 22.5% to A$52.1 million.
Part of that growth was bought.
Civmec acquired Luerssen Australia, now Civmec Defence Industries, in July 2025.
Infrastructure, Marine & Defence revenue more than doubled to A$210.2 million and Energy rose 62.1% while Resources, its largest segment, fell 8.4%.
Cash flow went the other way.
Free cash flow swung to an outflow of A$28.5 million from an inflow of A$56.1 million, as working capital and unbilled work in progress absorbed cash.
Civmec ended June with A$54.6 million in cash against A$60.0 million in borrowings, excluding lease liabilities.
The dividend held at A$0.060 per share for FY2026, and management points to a record order book.
Watch whether that work turns back into cash.
Related articles:
Passive Dividend Boost: 3 SGX Stocks Rewarding Investors in October 2026
Forget the Index: 3 SGX Small-Caps Beating the STI by Up to 51%
How is MoneyMax funding its expansion?
MoneyMax runs pawnbroking, gold and luxury retail, and secured lending in Singapore and Malaysia.
For 1H2026, revenue rose 34.1% YoY to S$325.7 million, while profit attributable to owners climbed 77.3% to S$52.5 million.
A bigger pawnbroking portfolio lifted interest income, and the retail arm sold more gold and luxury items.
Free cash flow, though, was an outflow of S$155.8 million, wider than the S$29.5 million outflow a year ago.
So where did the cash go?
Largely into new loans, as trade and other receivables grew by S$219.6 million.
A growing loan book consumes cash, and MoneyMax borrows to fund it.
Net debt stood at S$981.8 million at the end of June.
MoneyMax declared an interim dividend of S$0.0025 per share, after declaring none a year earlier, but free cash flow did not cover it.
The group has added 26 stores in 2026 and plans 10 more by year-end.
Management expects higher profit for FY2026, though softer consumer sentiment could weigh on gold retail.
Related articles:
Beyond STI: 3 Small-Cap Stocks Rewarding Dividend Investors in June 2026
Hidden Gems Punching Above Their Weight
Get Smart: Who pays for the growth?
Only two of these winners, Micro-Mechanics and Union Gas, generated the cash to pay for their expansion.
Civmec and MoneyMax consumed cash as they grew, and both now owe more than they hold in cash.
Neither path is wrong, but you’ll want to know which kind of company you own.
So before you buy a stock that has outrun the STI, open its
cash flow statement
.
Can the business fund its next leg of growth without borrowing more?
The answer tells you how much weight its dividend can bear.
You walk past million-dollar opportunities every single day. Your coffee shop. Your commute. Your grocery run. title: Alibaba chairman says open source is Europe’s best shot at AI
article:
(Oct 8): Alibaba Group Holding Ltd chairman Joe Tsai said open-source artificial intelligence (AI) is Europe’s best route to technological independence from the US and China, and urged the region to build out its own computing infrastructure to train and run AI models.

“No country would want to entirely trust another country’s technology: if there’s a change in government, a change in circumstances, they can just shut off the technology from you,” he said, speaking at the Wave by Vento conference in Turin, Italy, on Wednesday.

“What Europe needs to do is to get really serious about creating the compute infrastructure to allow these models to run, to train the models and run inference on Europe-based infrastructure,” he continued, referring to the process of running AI systems after they’ve been trained.

He added that Europe isn’t making the most of its AI researchers, who are often highly sought after by US and Chinese labs. Europe should focus on training AI models on proprietary industrial data to gain an edge, he said.

Factories in China “have very valuable manufacturing data, and all that data can be quite valuable in training models”, he said. “In many countries in Europe, we still have large industrial bases here.”

Tsai said he is bullish on Europe’s raft of so-called neoclouds, specialised cloud-computing firms that operate data centres kitted out with AI chips.

See also: MAS sets AI risk expectations for financial institutions in Singapore

He added that China is intentionally focused on open-source models and publishing research to boost uptake globally, contrasting this unfavourably with the proprietary models mostly offered by US firms such as OpenAI and Anthropic PBC.

“The American labs, closed-source labs, they don’t write papers any more because they don’t want to share,” he said. “They want to be closed.”

title: Singapore bank shares tumble as yield surge threatens earnings
article:
(Oct 8): A sell-off in Singapore bank shares deepened after JPMorgan Chase & Co warned that surging long bond yields will hurt third-quarter earnings for Southeast Asian lenders.

DBS Group Holdings Ltd and United Overseas Bank Ltd fell more than 5% each, while Oversea-Chinese Banking Corp dropped as much as 4.8%. They were the biggest drags on the benchmark Straits Times Index, which tumbled 3.5%, the most since April 2025. The index was the worst performer in Asia.

The drop comes after a years-long rally in Singapore lenders driven by record profits and the city-state’s growing stature as a global wealth hub. That supportive backdrop is now being tested by concerns over the impact of high bond yields on dividend payouts, with valuations elevated.

“What matters is not just where rates are going, but whether asset yields can keep pace with rising funding costs to defend net interest margins,” said James Ooi, market strategist at Tiger Brokers in Singapore. While higher rates can lift yields on loans and other assets, banks’ profitability also depends on the levels lenders pay for deposits and other forms of funding, he said.

On Wednesday, a JPMorgan analyst said surging long bond yields will lead to higher mark-to-market losses on trading books and hit capital market activity for Southeast Asian banks. In Singapore, slower balance-sheet growth, rising deposit competition and a potential normalisation in wealth-management fees could trigger earnings downgrades, with OCBC more at risk.

See also: UOB launches online branch appointment booking system for over 25 services

“The surprise getting into third quarter 2026 is likely skewed negative for quite a few banks under our coverage,” JPMorgan analyst Harsh Wardhan Modi wrote in a note, recommending clients trim their allocations.

The rally earlier this year also left Singapore banks looking expensive relative to some Wall Street rivals, including Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs. DBS, the country’s largest lender, trades at 2.9 times one-year forward book value, nearly double its historical average.

See also: HSBC’s new trading floor has far less headroom than rivals

Singapore banks have been the biggest beneficiaries of measures by the Singapore Exchange Ltd and Monetary Authority of Singapore to improve corporate performance and broaden investor interest, said Kieran Calder, who covers global banks as head of Asia equity research at Union Bancaire Privee. Strong underlying domestic economic growth and banks’ increased focus on fee income also helped, he said.

The sell-off has been amplified by a broader rotation out of lenders. Global banks were among the biggest beneficiaries of last quarter’s retreat from artificial intelligence-related stocks, leaving the sector vulnerable as that trade unwinds.

“There are renewed fears of inflation and it would put a dampener on some of the investment cases in some of the banks,” said Nirgunan Tiruchelvam, an analyst at Aletheia Capital. Higher bond yields will put the focus on emerging market sectors facing vulnerabilities, including Singapore banks, he said.

title: Vodafone boosts cost-cutting target for UK to £1 bil by 2032
article:
(Oct 8): Vodafone Group plc said its UK business would save costs of £1 billion annually by fiscal 2032, upgrading its outlook after taking full control of the business earlier this year.

The update follows “strong progress” against VodafoneThree’s initial cost targets, the company said on Thursday. Vodafone also increased the unit’s savings target for the fiscal year ending in March 2030 to £800 million from £700 million per year.

The new goalposts mark the first significant update since Vodafone’s full buyout of VodafoneThree earlier this year. The operator after the merger of UK businesses owned by Vodafone and CK Hutchison Holdings Ltd in 2025.

The buyout is part of Vodafone chief executive officer Margherita Della Valle’s push to streamline the broader group’s operations, focusing on key markets while divesting from others. In the UK, the extra savings will come from shutting down overlapping sites and upgrading the two networks to be more efficient, the company said. It also expects to bring in more revenue.

Vodafone’s shares fell 0.6% to 126.95 pence at 8.26am on Thursday. The stock has gained about 28% this year.

title: Bank of France’s Moulin says all countries now facing higher rates
article:
(Oct 8): Bank of France governor Emmanuel Moulin said that the geopolitical shock of the Middle East crisis is hitting all economies, even those with stronger public finances.

A member of the European Central Bank’s Governing Council, he cited the impact of inflation on global bond yields while skirting any immediate reference to the troubles faced by his own country.

“We see that there is a strong correlation between oil, long-term interest rates in the US, and interest rates in Europe,” he said on Thursday in Istanbul. “This increase in interest rates affects all countries, whatever is their fiscal position. Actually some countries with very strong fiscal positions are affected, as countries with weaker fiscal positions.”

Moulin spoke in a month when France has been in the sights of investors over its struggles to pass a budget and narrow its bloated deficit in turbulence that sparked memories of the eurozone debt crisis. Earlier on Thursday, Finance Minister Roland Lescure insisted that the country has no problem selling its bonds.

“What we see is that this geopolitical shock is also transmitting into a financial shock, and this is, I think, an important point to keep in mind,” Moulin said. “Financial conditions have been impacted by the increase in interest rates.”

He also observed that consumer-price growth driven by the oil and gas shock hasn’t spread much beyond that category.

See also: WTO chief sees urgent need to harden supply lines as world frays

“It’s clearly 100% energy,” Moulin said. “We see very little indirect effect. We see very small impact at this stage, and we don’t see second-round effects.”

Speaking at the same event, his Dutch counterpart, Olaf Sleijpen, echoed that observation, adding that while the energy shock is “quite persistent,” households’ inflation expectations are well anchored.

title: Behind Zara billionaire’s modest lifestyle is a growing fortune
article:
(Oct 8): Sandra Ortega, Spain’s richest woman, has spent most of her life in the small northwestern town of Oleiros, a windy place overlooking the Atlantic Ocean.

The 58-year-old is so intensely private and lives such an ordinary life that “for all they have,” there’s little that points to her immense wealth, says Ángel García Seoane, the town’s mayor.

The second-largest shareholder of Zara owner Inditex SA after her father, the company’s founder Amancio Ortega, Sandra’s 5.05% stake is currently valued at about €8.5 billion (US$9.5 billion or $12.2 billion). Her half-sister Marta, Inditex’s chairwoman, is the more visible member of the next generation of Ortegas. But Sandra, Amancio’s daughter with his first wife, has amassed enormous wealth without ever playing a role at the business her parents started — now the world’s biggest fashion retailer.

When 90-year-old Amancio, whose net worth stands at about US$127 billion, eventually passes on, Sandra’s wealth is set to grow substantially. Under local laws, at least a quarter of his estate’s value will go to his descendants. That would give his three children — Sandra, her disabled brother Marcos and Marta — a minimum of US$10.6 billion each, based on Bloomberg Billionaires Index’s estimate of his fortune. The inheritance may not necessarily be in Inditex shares, but Sandra’s current stake already gives her unusual clout.

Sandra’s only direct connection to Inditex’s operations has been through her husband, who has held low-profile jobs at the company linked to facilities and innovation. Her three young-adult children have not been involved in the business, and there’s little to suggest that will change after Amancio Ortega. But Amancio’s descendants from his two marriages have had almost no relationship for decades, leaving investors with the question of how Inditex’s family shareholders will deal with one another once he — their common link — is no longer in the picture.

“The vulnerability is not today; it is the day Amancio Ortega’s shares move,” said Martin Roll, a global family business strategist and senior adviser at McKinsey & Co. “A passive shareholder with a meaningfully larger stake, no board seat and no track record of how she would vote when it matters becomes a strategic variable for everyone around the table, including outside investors.”

See also: MAS may include insurance policies, digital payment tokens as Designated Investment assets for single family offices

Granted, Amancio may already have in place an ownership architecture for the nearly 60% stake in Inditex held by his holding firm Pontegadea, with a well-defined shareholders’ pact and family governance structure that has not been made public. Still, how family shareholders work together is often critical to such companies’ future, said Alfonso Chiner, a professor at IESE who specialises in such entities.

“The shareholders of a family business need commitment and unity,” he said. “The predecessor, successor, the company and the family all have to comply with a joint, parallel and organised plan.”

Spokespeople for Sandra’s organisations, Inditex and Pontegadea declined to comment. Sandra didn’t accept requests for a meeting and didn’t make any of her staff available for interviews. But conversations with about a dozen people familiar with her world paint a picture of a reluctant billionaire who shuns the trappings of the rich even as Inditex continues to swell her coffers.

See also: HSBC taps growing demand from HNW entrepreneurs with launch of Access in Singapore

Inditex is headquartered in Arteixo, just outside A Coruña, a port city of sandy beaches and cobbled streets where Amancio Ortega lives in a 19th-century building with glass-enclosed balconies overlooking the shoreline. Nearby, a similar façade houses Sandra’s family office.

Although a short distance sets the two buildings apart, father and daughter were long estranged, a reflection of the family rupture that shaped Sandra's place in the Inditex story.

More than four decades ago, her parents separated after Amancio’s relationship with an Inditex employee, Flora Pérez, resulted in the birth of a daughter — Marta. His two families had little to do with each other. Over time, however, Amancio and Sandra have rebuilt a relationship, people familiar with the matter said, declining to be named discussing private matters.

The story of Sandra’s fortune, which she now manages through her family office and a foundation, traces its roots to the creation of Zara by her parents in the mid-1970s.

Sandra’s mother, Rosalía Mera, was born in 1944 in A Coruña and grew up in poverty. Mera’s home faced a beach where a slaughterhouse sewer emptied blood and scraps into the sea. Leaving school at 11, Mera took up jobs as a seamstress to support her family, eventually working at a haberdashery known as La Maja, where she met her future husband, Amancio Ortega.

In the beginning, they were a team of four: Mera, Amancio, his brother Antonio and sister-in-law Primitiva Renedo, according to the Zara founders’ biographer Xabier Blanco. Mera and Renedo began sewing baby buntings, but it was a women’s padded housecoat — a cheaper version of a popular design — that became their breakout product. Production spread beyond Renedo’s home to a network of women sewing from workshops and homes, while Amancio and Antonio handled sales and distribution.

Mera and Amancio had two children: Sandra, in 1968, and Marcos, born three years later with cerebral palsy. Mera soon assumed caregiving responsibilities while Amancio threw himself into the business. After a failed first attempt, they launched Zara in 1975, the flagship brand of what is today Inditex. As the business expanded through the late 1970s, the couple’s relationship deteriorated. By 1984, they split up after Amancio had formed a new family with Pérez and Marta.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

After their separation, Mera remained one of Inditex’s principal shareholders, even as her ownership declined over the years. Although she was largely removed from the company’s day-to-day operations, she remained a dedicated and opinionated board member, her biographer Blanco said. By the time of its public listing in 2001, Inditex had become enormous, with its valuation running into the billions. Mera sold half her position, keeping 7% and remaining the second-largest holder after Amancio. Mera stepped down as board member in 2004, and when she died in 2013, Sandra inherited her stake.

Sandra largely followed in the footsteps of her mother, who had turned to philanthropy as her connection to Inditex faded. Mera defended abortion rights and focused on issues like education and social inclusion. Headstrong, she sparked a small outcry in 2011 when she publicly supported the “Indignados,” an anti-establishment grassroots movement that emerged after the financial crisis.

Despite her fortune, Mera was seen as austere, zipping around town in a small hatchback bearing the insignia of one of her organisations and negotiating every penny. Her stance on wealth was coloured by her childhood, says Antonio Pernas, a designer from A Coruña born the same year as Mera. Since emigrants returning from the Americas sometimes came dressed in bright colors and patterned scarves to show off their newfound prosperity, anyone clothed a little extravagantly would be mocked with shouts of “¡Hay barco!” — “The boat’s in!” — suggesting they were like the newly rich returnees, he said. Mera remained wary of ostentatious displays of wealth all her life.

“Sandra is even more obsessed than her mother with making sure nobody could tell they were rich,” said Pancho Casal, a film producer whose company Mera had backed.

The only photos of Sandra online are from her mother’s funeral more than a decade ago.

Her childhood was spent in a middle-class neighbourhood of A Coruña. Around the time her parents separated, she asked to swap her catholic education for a state school on the other side of town, where she met her husband. She studied psychology at a public university before joining Paideia, a charitable foundation created by her mother for social transformation.

For all that, Sandra’s family office Rosp, which stands for Rosalía Patrimonio, has continued to make high-profile bets across the world. Its profit grew 2% to €307 million in 2025, according to the most recent accounts available, and its assets were valued at over €11 billion. Her three children joined the family office’s board in 2024.

Rosp’s largest holding is its Inditex stake, which will rake in €275 million in dividends this year. It also owns a 5% of PharmaMar, a small Spanish company that specializes in oncology treatments, and invests in a broad range of venture capital and private equity funds that are mostly based in Spain. Although Sandra has avoided the lifestyle of the rich and famous, over the years her family office has built a vast portfolio of high-end hotels and real estate across the globe.

”That is not a woman who is uninterested in money,” said McKinsey’s Roll.

Rosp’s holdings include such iconic hotels as the Waldorf Towers on Miami beach, a 1937 art deco-style building on Ocean Drive, and Palo-Alto’s El Prado, a hotel whose storied Italian eatery counted Steve Jobs, Jeff Bezos and Mark Zuckerberg among customers before closing this year. It bought the Radisson Blu on Leicester Square in London for €142 million a few months ago. In Portugal, Rosp has spent more than a decade backing the development of Na Praia, a luxury resort of villas and hotel suites overlooking one of the country’s most exclusive stretches of coastline.

Although Sandra has a small team running the show at her family office, she’s not entirely hands-off. That was demonstrated by her 2020 decision to fire its chief investment officer, who had worked first for her mother and then for her. Sandra later accused him of misappropriation and disloyal administration, among other things, drawing her into a series of legal battles.

Her own activities revolve around the charitable foundation, which had a budget of about €3.5 million last year.

Sandra rarely makes public appearances, even when it involves her foundation. Under the “contact” tab, her foundation’s website states that its president “does not maintain profiles or engage in any activity on social media,” nor does she take part in “any public dialogue regarding social or philanthropic initiatives, business activities, or any other type of endeavour.”

She provided a rare glimpse into her view on life when a park named after her mother was inaugurated in Oleiros in 2024. Financed by her, it preserved old trees, stone walls and uneven ground and included over 200 plant species, nest boxes for birds and a pond full of a croaky frogs. Certain areas in the park are not lit at night to protect the circadian cycles of animals. In a documentary on the park a year later, Sandra reminisced about her childhood and mulled over creating “a green space instead of building homes.”

“I think this is a space that allows people to pause and be in the world, for a little moment, in a different way,” she said in voiceover at the end of the film.

title: Reliance may be a cheaper way to buy Jio after its listing
article:
(Oct 8): Reliance Industries Ltd may offer investors a cheaper way to own Jio Platforms Ltd after the telecom unit lists, with analysts saying the parent company’s shares reflect a substantial discount.

Reliance’s share price implies a roughly 36% discount on its two-thirds stake in Jio, according to Nimish Maheshwari, co-founder of independent research firm Beat The Street. He sees about 25% as sustainable, in line with how the market values telecom rival Bharti Airtel Ltd’s holdings in its listed subsidiaries.

Such discounts are common for parent companies because their shareholders only get indirect exposure to the businesses they own. Once a subsidiary lists, investors can simply buy its shares directly.

While these discounts could go as high as 50%, there’s no strong technical or fundamental justification for such a steep discount here, said Thea Jamison, managing director at Change Global Investment. “Moreover, how Reliance Industries chooses to monetise its stake in Jio Platforms going forward could be another significant source of value creation for shareholders.”

Jio may seek a valuation of about 11 trillion rupees (US$114 billion) in an initial public offering as soon as this month, Bloomberg News reported. That would value Reliance’s stake at about 7.3 trillion rupees, equivalent to about 45% of the parent’s current market value, according to Bloomberg calculations.

Yet brokerages including Motilal Oswal, Yes Securities and Nuvama value the stake at 331 to 450 rupees per Reliance share, implying it accounts for around 27% to 37% of the parent’s share price.

See also: Japan 30-year bond sale sees firmer demand than 12-month average

Reliance shares have fallen 23% this year, compared with a 14% decline in the benchmark Nifty 50 Index, as higher oil prices, elevated global bond yields and a weaker rupee weigh on Indian equities. The conglomerate controlled by billionaire Mukesh Ambani is particularly exposed to those pressures with its businesses spanning energy, consumer spending and capital-intensive sectors.

The potential upside for Reliance shareholders from any narrowing of the discount will depend on how Jio trades after its debut.

“The key trigger would be transparent price discovery rather than immediate monetisation,” Maheshwari said. “A higher public-market valuation for Jio Platforms would increase the visible value of RIL’s holding and could, in turn, help narrow the holding-company discount.”

See also: US court allows fund to obtain documents in Radiant World case

A clearer separation of Jio’s valuation would also make Reliance’s remaining businesses easier for investors to assess, said Chokkalingam G, founder of Equinomics Research. He expects the listing to help drive a rerating as investors begin valuing Reliance’s underlying businesses more distinctly.

title: Samsung profit up almost nine-fold with memory chip windfall
article:
(Oct 8): Samsung Electronics Co reported a nearly nine-fold rise in quarterly operating profit, though that was still shy of sky-high expectations elevated by relentless spending on AI infrastructure.

The world’s largest memory chipmaker posted a record preliminary operating profit of 107.4 trillion won (US$80.1 billion or $100 billion) for the quarter through September. But even those record results still fell short of the average analyst forecast. Revenue came to 195 trillion won, also lower than expectations. Shares erased early gains in Seoul trading on Thursday to fall as much as 2.1%.

“Samsung has delivered a record profit and still fallen short of expectations, which tells you just how demanding the AI trade has become,” said Josh Gilbert, lead Asia Pacific analyst at eToro.

Technology providers are rushing to secure supplies of memory needed to power AI services. High-bandwidth memory — the critical chips used alongside Nvidia Corp and other AI accelerators — is drawing massive spending, with flash memory and low-power chips also in demand. The record numbers and high expectations underscore how sharply the economics of the AI boom have swung in favour of Samsung, SK Hynix Inc and Micron Technology Inc.

Counterpoint Research raised its forecast for third-quarter DRAM prices to a 10% to 20% sequential increase, from 5% to 10% previously, saying customers are bringing forward orders.

See also: DeepSeek to raise at least US$12 bil in Tencent-backed funding

“Samsung is quite undervalued right now,” said Neil Shah, vice president of research at Counterpoint. “They’ve got a lot up their sleeve for next year with HBM, mostly because the full effect hasn’t even landed yet.”

Citigroup analysts Peter Lee and Jayden Oh echoed that optimism, predicting 12-layer HBM4 prices could jump 100% to 150% next year, significantly boosting Samsung’s average selling prices and profit margins — although the brokerage has cut its full-year profit forecast for the company due to a stronger Korean won.

The boom has transformed Samsung’s semiconductor business, which only a few years ago was grappling with losses after a punishing downturn in demand. Now, the AI infrastructure buildout is absorbing vast amounts of advanced DRAM, while Samsung is gaining ground on SK Hynix in HBM. The strength of the cycle is also showing up in South Korea’s trade data, with semiconductor exports more than tripling from a year earlier in September.

See also: Musk is a trillionaire again as SpaceX claws back post-IPO slump

Analysts on average estimate Samsung’s chip division will post operating profit of 110 trillion won while its electronics unit will report a loss. The Suwon-based company will release a full financial statement on Oct 29.

Market caution persists, however. Samsung’s shares remain about 25% below their June peak even after the company reported record-breaking results in July. Investors retain a measure of scepticism around soaring profits in a sector prone to boom-and-bust cycles. Samsung and SK Hynix are now expanding production capacity while also increasingly backing companies in the AI sector in a bid to drive more demand for their products.

Highlighting current market dynamics, Advanced Micro Devices Inc chief executive officer Lisa Su emphasised long-term strategic partnerships with both Samsung and SK Hynix during a visit to Seoul this week. Su confirmed AMD has begun shipping its next-generation Instinct MI455X and Helios systems featuring HBM4.

“Memory is so essential to overall computing; it has been a very tight supply environment,” Su told reporters, adding AMD’s HBM partnerships with Samsung and SK Hynix will span multiple product generations. “We’re encouraging our partners to build as fast as possible.”

title: WTO chief sees urgent need to harden supply lines as world frays
article:
(Oct 8): World trade is facing its sternest test in eight decades and must reimagine supply lines to guarantee resilience in the face of an increasingly fragmented globe, according to the head of the World Trade Organization.

“This is an unprecedented time for global trade,” Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala said in an interview on Bloomberg Television with Francine Lacqua. “We are seeing disruptions to trade, emerging fragmentation, in a way we’ve not seen since really eighty years.”

The body has been under intense scrutiny as US President Donald Trump’s on-again-off-again tariffs on trading partners challenge WTO norms and provoke questions about how the three-decade-old organisation operates.

“Many members of the WTO are beginning to feel that the rules no longer work for them,” said Okonjo-Iweala, a former Nigerian finance minister.

Conflict in the Middle East has also disrupted critical sea routes for vital supplies of fuel, sparking an energy crisis and hammering home the need for diversification.

“Instead of being dependent on one geography or one place,” production should be decentralised to other places with a comparative advantage, Okonjo-Iweala said. It won’t be easy “but the world needs to begin now and there’s some of that happening,” she said.

See also: We have to thank the bond markets for telling the truth: Tharman

title: Japan 30-year bond sale sees firmer demand than 12-month average
article:
(Oct 8): Japan’s 30-year government bond auction drew stronger demand than its 12-month average as elevated yields attracted investors.

The bid-to-cover ratio at Thursday’s sale was 3.88 compared with 3.79 at the previous auction and a 12-month average of 3.56. Japan’s bonds were steady after the sale.

Global bonds have been under pressure due to inflation concerns triggered by the US-Iran war and amid worries about worsening government finances. Japan’s 30-year yield hit its highest level since its debut this week.

Investors are cautious about fiscal policy in Japan as Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi seeks to enact a bill to cut the sales tax on food and soft drinks, while questions remain over how it will be funded without the issuance of additional debt. The Japanese government is also considering compiling a second supplementary budget in fiscal 2026, Yomiuri reported.

Japan’s 10-year government bond auction Tuesday saw solid demand as elevated yields underpinned buying. Long-term bond yields in the US also pared their rise on Wednesday after a sale of 10-year notes signalled that rates at multidecade highs were fuelling investor appetite.
